title: 2 Samuel 20:14–22
context: Sheba passes through the tribes of Israel to Abel of Beth Maacah, and Joab’s army besieges the city and begins battering its wall. A wise woman calls to Joab from the wall, appeals to the city’s reputation for wise counsel, and asks why he would swallow up the LORD’s inheritance. Joab replies that he seeks only Sheba, and the woman persuades her people to hand over Sheba’s head, so the city is spared and Joab returns to Jerusalem. The identity of the Berites in verse 14 is uncertain, and the Hebrew written text there can be read as they cursed him, though the margin reading and ancient versions have they were gathered together; in verse 19 the ancient Greek wording differs slightly, without changing the overall sense. Arminian and Reformed readers commonly treat the wise woman as shared ground: a peacemaker whose wisdom saves many lives (compare Ecclesiastes 9:15).

verses.text: He went through all the tribes of Israel to Abel, to Beth Maacah, and all the Berites. They were gathered together, and went also after him.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Sheba passing through the tribes to Abel of Beth Maacah, with others gathering after him. The pursuit narrows.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as moving the story toward its climax at Abel. Readers in both traditions commonly hold the identification of the Berites with caution.

verses.text: They came and besieged him in Abel of Beth Maacah, and they cast up a mound against the city, and it stood against the rampart; and all the people who were with Joab battered the wall to throw it down.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Joab’s army besieging the city, building a mound, and battering the wall. The city faces destruction.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the siege as threatening many innocent lives because of one rebel. Both traditions commonly read the verse as setting up the need for wise intervention.

verses.text: Then a wise woman cried out of the city, “Hear, hear! Please say to Joab, ‘Come near here, that I may speak with you.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see a wise woman calling out from the city and asking to speak with Joab. Wisdom takes initiative in a crisis.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see her as another wise woman in Samuel (compare 2 Samuel 14:2). Readers in both traditions commonly honor her courage in speaking to an army commander.

verses.text: He came near to her; and the woman said, “Are you Joab?” He answered, “I am.” Then she said to him, “Hear the words of your servant.” He answered, “I’m listening.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the woman confirming Joab’s identity and asking him to listen. She opens with respect and real clarity.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see her careful approach as wise diplomacy. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a model of seeking a hearing before conflict escalates.

verses.text: Then she spoke, saying, “They used to say in old times, ‘They shall surely ask counsel at Abel,’ and so they settled a matter.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the woman recalling that Abel was known for wise counsel that settled matters. She appeals to the city’s heritage.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see her reminder as urging Joab to seek counsel before destruction (compare Proverbs 11:14). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as valuing wisdom over force.

verses.text: I am among those who are peaceable and faithful in Israel. You seek to destroy a city and a mother in Israel. Why will you swallow up the LORD’s inheritance?”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the woman calling herself peaceable and faithful, and asking why Joab would swallow up the LORD’s inheritance. She defends her city boldly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see her appeal as grounding the city’s worth in its place among God’s people. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a powerful plea for mercy (compare Deuteronomy 20:10).

verses.text: Joab answered, “Far be it, far be it from me, that I should swallow up or destroy.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Joab denying that he wants to destroy the city. He responds to her appeal and insists that destruction is not his aim.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see his emphatic denial as opening the way for peace. Readers in both traditions commonly see the verse as the turning point of the negotiation.

verses.text: The matter is not so. But a man of the hill country of Ephraim, Sheba the son of Bichri by name, has lifted up his hand against the king, even against David. Just deliver him, and I will depart from the city.” The woman said to Joab, “Behold, his head will be thrown to you over the wall.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Joab explaining that he seeks only Sheba, and the woman promising that his head will be thrown over the wall. A solution emerges.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the agreement as limiting bloodshed to the one who led the revolt. Both traditions commonly read the verse as wisdom finding a way to save the many.

verses.text: Then the woman went to all the people in her wisdom. They cut off the head of Sheba the son of Bichri, and threw it out to Joab. He blew the trumpet, and they were dispersed from the city, every man to his tent. Then Joab returned to Jerusalem to the king.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the woman persuading her people, Sheba’s head being thrown to Joab, and the army departing. Wisdom saves the city.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the outcome as fulfilling her role as a peacemaker (compare Matthew 5:9; Ecclesiastes 9:15). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse soberly, noting both the deliverance and the violence that ended the revolt.
